newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish political, military leaders in key meeting.
newsitem.headline: Turkish political, military leaders in key meeting.

text.p: Turkey's political leaders prepared on Friday for much-awaited talks with the military elite expected to focus on increasing strains between the Islamist-led government and the secular establishment.
The National Security Council, chaired by President Suleyman Demirel and grouping senior commanders and ministers, was due to meet at 3.00 p.m. (1300 GMT).
Political analysts expect the council, dominated by secularist officers, to issue a warning to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan that mounting Islamist zeal threatens Turkey's democratic institutions.

Ahead of the meeting, the Turkish media carried reports of a letter -- dismissed as untrue by Erbakan and President Suleyman Demirel's office -- that Demirel had warned the Islamist-led coalition against threatening Turkey's "secularist, democratic (and) republican aims".
The reports, echoing Demirel's recent briefings to newspaper editors, aggravated political tensions over the rising profile of Islamists in the Moslem but secular state.
Those strains have escalated since the army sent tanks on manoeuvres through the Ankara district of Sincan early in February following an Islamist protest there attended by the Iranian ambassador.

"The fear that the rising tension of recent days will lead to the burning bridges, however unlikely, has been enough to make everybody's hair stand on end in Ankara," wrote Bilal Cetin, columnist for the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil.

Speaking after regular talks with Demirel on Thursday evening, Erbakan dismissed claims that the Islamist-secularist row was undermining his eight-month-old coalition with the True Path Party of pro-western Tansu Ciller.
"Thankfully our government is working harmoniously. The censure motions helped to strengthen our government further," Erbakan told reporters after the talks.

His government this week survived a censure motion challenge from two leftist parties who said the coalition was a threat to the country's secularism. Next week in parliament, it will face another censure motion debate proposed by the leading opposition party.
Military displeasure at Erbakan's efforts to push ahead with Islam-based policies is not expected to result in anything like the three army interventions seen in Turkey since 1960, analysts said.
Financial markets remained steady in cautious trading ahead of the National Security Council meeting.
